nodes.name: Ni-EDTA Complex Formation
nodes.procedure: A solution was prepared by dissolving 3.32 g (11 mmol) of Ni(NO3)2‧6H2O in 40 mL of DMF, followed by the addition of 3 mL (21.6 mmol) of triethylamine and 1.18 g (4 mmol) of H4EDTA dissolved in 60 mL of DMF. The resulting mixture was stirred for 1 h to form a precipitate, which was subsequently washed three times with DMF by centrifugation. After drying under vacuum at 60 °C overnight, an aquamarine powder of 2.06 g was obtained.
nodes.source_text: Synthesis of [Ni2(EDTA)]n ... an aquamarine powder of 2.06 g was obtained.

nodes.name: Ni@NC Pyrolysis and Acid Etching
nodes.procedure: 2 g of [Ni2(EDTA)]n was finely ground and placed in a tube furnace for pyrolysis. It was heated under an Ar atmosphere at a rate of 5 °C min-1 until reaching 1000 °C, followed by dwelling at this temperature for 1 h. After naturally cooling, a black powder (552.8 mg) was obtained. This powder was then dispersed in a mixed solution of 1 M FeCl3·6H2O (28 mL) and 1 M HCl (22 mL) at 80 °C and stirred for 12 h. After cooling, the precipitated solid was washed with ultrapure water several times until a near-neutral centrifugate was achieved. Finally, it underwent vacuum drying at 60 °C overnight to yield a black powder product (171.3 mg).

nodes.name: RuNi/NC Kirkendall Alloying
nodes.procedure: 30 mg of Ni@NC and 5 mg of RuCl3·xH2O were combined in 20 mL of distilled water and stirred overnight. Then the resulting mixture underwent drying in an oven at 80 °C for 10 h. The ensuing dried powder was subjected to calcination in a tube furnace under an Ar atmosphere enriched with 5% H2. The heating process proceeded at a rate of 5 °C min-1 to 1000 °C and was maintained at this temperature for 2 h, followed by natural cooling to yield the final black powder product (21.3 mg).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni@NC shows buried Ni nanoparticles with average size ca. 10 nm within onion-like multilayered graphitic nanocarbons.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Transmission electron microscope (TEM) analysis of the intermediary Ni@NC reveals the presence of buried Ni nanoparticles with an average size of ca. 10 nm within the onion-like multilayered graphitic nanocarbons (Fig. 1b, c and Supplementary Fig. 2).

nodes.characterization_summary: MNi/NC shows hollow carbon nanocages with shell thicknesses 2-3 nm, diameters 5-10 nm, curvature radii 2.1-6.0 nm, external surfaces adorned with protruding Ni-based bimetallic nanoalloys.
nodes.evidence_snippet: In contrast, TEM images of MNi/NC clearly illustrate the formation of hollow carbon nanocages, characterized by shell thicknesses ranging from 2 to 3 nm and diameters spanning 5-10 nm, with curvature radii varying from 2.1 to 6.0 nm (Supplementary Fig. 3).

nodes.characterization_summary: HAADF-STEM mapping exhibits evenly distributed bimetallic elements within MNi/NC nanoalloys.
nodes.evidence_snippet: High-angle annular dark field (HAADF) scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) mapping exhibits the evenly distributed bimetallic elements within these nanoalloys (Fig. 1d‒m and Supplementary Figs. 4–8).

nodes.characterization_summary: AC-STEM reveals lattice atomic arrangements corresponding to Ru1.68Ni0.32 (hexagonal), PtNi3 (cubic), Pd0.19Ni0.81 (cubic), CuNi3 (cubic), and Zn0.08Ni0.92 (cubic).
nodes.evidence_snippet: atomic-resolution HAADF imaging using aberration-corrected STEM (AC-STEM) reveals well-matched lattice atomic arrangements corresponding to Ru1.68Ni0.32 (hexagonal), PtNi3 (cubic), Pd0.19Ni0.81 (cubic) and CuNi3 (cubic) and Zn0.08Ni0.92 (cubic)

nodes.characterization_summary: Metal contents of MNi/NC determined by ICP-AES, with RuNi/NC showing lower Ni content.
nodes.evidence_snippet: their metal contents determined by inductively coupled plasma-atomic emission spectrometry (ICP–AES) are presented in Supplementary Table 1

nodes.characterization_summary: XRD confirms phase structures: RuNi/NC shows hexagonal Ru1.68Ni0.32 and residual cubic Ni; other MNi/NC exhibit cubic alloy structures matching standards; all show attenuated graphite (002) peak at 26°.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The definitive phase structures of these nanoalloys were corroborated through X-ray diffraction (XRD) analysis (Fig. 1n). Except for RuNi/NC, which shows diffraction peaks corresponding to hexagonal Ru1.68Ni0.32 and residual cubic Ni, all other MNi/NC samples exhibit similar patterns to Ni@NC and match well with the standard patterns of their respective cubic alloy structures.

nodes.characterization_summary: MNi/NC catalysts exhibit super-hydrophilic surfaces with water contact angles <10° vs Ni@NC.
nodes.evidence_snippet: after Kirkendall alloying, all MNi/NC samples exhibit enhanced water affinity compared to Ni@NC, as evidenced by their super-hydrophilic characters with low water contact angles <10° (Fig. 1o and Supplementary Fig. 9).

nodes.characterization_summary: RuNi/NC shows uniform dispersion of RuNi nanoalloys with mean diameter of 2 nm on carbon nanocages.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The STEM image presented in Fig. 2a clearly shows the uniform dispersion of RuNi nanoalloys on carbon nanocages, exhibiting a mean diameter of 2 nm

nodes.characterization_summary: RuNi/NC shows well-defined lattice atomic arrangement characteristic of hexagonal P63/mmc Ru1.68Ni0.32 alloy oriented along [10-11] zone axis.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The well-defined lattice atomic arrangement, characteristic of the hexagonal P63/mmc Ru1.68Ni0.32 alloy oriented along the [10-11] zone axis

nodes.characterization_summary: RuNi/NC measured specific surface area 326.3 m² g⁻¹ and total pore volume 1.18 cm³ g⁻¹.
nodes.evidence_snippet: This observation is further attested by the high specific surface area (326.3 m² g⁻¹) and total pore volume (1.18 cm³ g⁻¹) of RuNi/NC, as measured by N₂ isothermal sorption (Supplementary Fig. 12).

nodes.characterization_summary: Ni K-edge XANES shows RuNi/NC between Ni foil and NiO (metallic Ni in Ni@NC), indicating intermediate Ni valence 0-+2 from electron transfer to Ru; Ru K-edge aligns with Ru foil.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Figure 2g illustrates that the X-ray absorption near edge structure (XANES) spectroscopy reveals nearly coincident Ni K-edges for Ni@NC and Ni foil... the Ni K-edge of RuNi/NC is situated between those of Ni foil and NiO... the Ru K-edge XANES spectrum of RuNi/NC aligns with that of Ru foil (Fig. 2i)

nodes.characterization_summary: RuNi/NC Ni K-edge shows Ni-Ru/Ni-Ni at 2.15 Å and Ni-N at 1.56 Å; Ru K-edge shows Ru-Ni/Ru-Ru at 2.33 Å.
nodes.evidence_snippet: The Ni K-edge EXAFS spectrum shows a prominent peak at 2.15 Å, attributed to Ni–Ru and Ni–Ni bonds, while a fainter peak at 1.56 Å corresponds to the Ni–N bond... the Ru K-edge EXAFS of RuNi/NC reveals a significant peak at 2.33 Å, indicative of Ru–Ni and Ru–Ru bonds

nodes.characterization_summary: Raman verifies graphitic structure of carbon nanocages in RuNi/NC.
nodes.evidence_snippet: Their graphitic structure is verified by Raman spectra

nodes.characterization_summary: XPS analysis consistent with XAS showing electron transfer from Ni to Ru in RuNi/NC.
nodes.evidence_snippet: a finding that is consistent with the X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) analysis (Supplementary Figs. 14–16)
